captions.text: Now, contrast this miserable experience with the strategy of
treating the gatekeeper as the actual VIP.
And here's what that means for you.
This is a massive blind spot for most professionals.
They view assistants and secretaries as obstacles to
be bypassed. But recognizing the humanity
of the gatekeeper, elevating the assistant before
you even attempt to reach the executive secures long-term
structural loyalty where transactional networking
completely fails. They aren't just obstacles.
Secretaries, assistants, and spouses have names.
They have rich internal lives.
And most importantly, they have absolute veto power
over your access. The book offers a very
specific almost theatrical tactic for this called
the hoham caper. I love the name of this
one. Instead of calling and formally asking, "Hello, may
I please speak to Miss Bigshot?" which instantly
identifies you as an outsider seeking favor, you
dial the number and casually let the pronoun roll
off your tongue with a sigh.
Hi, Bob Smith here.
Is she in? Is she in?
Yeah, but if I try that, I feel like
I'm committing corporate fraud.
Fraud. Dropping a casual is she in is a
deliberate attempt to deceive the secretary.
You're spoofing your social status to bypass security protocols.
You're manipulating them into thinking you're a personal friend
of the boss. And when the boss picks up
and says, "Who is this?" The jig is entirely
up. You are interpreting it as a lie, but
it is actually a refusal to submit to an
artificial class system. How so?
